analysis.one_liner: Approves the Keystone XL pipeline, speeds oil and gas leasing on federal land, and delays EPA air rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2012 with 31 Republican Senate sponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have approved the Keystone XL oil pipeline without a presidential permit, barred the EPA from finalizing several air-pollution rules until months after a new government study, and required faster oil and gas leasing on federal land with fewer environmental reviews. It also pushed oil development in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve, put a temporary hold on coal-mining regulations, launched a critical-minerals program, and included narrower help for offshore wind testing.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, pipeline builders like TransCanada, coal operators, and petroleum refiners. Renewable developers got smaller benefits: faster permitting for offshore wind test towers and dedicated funding for solar and wind right-of-way reviews.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and refining companies

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no presidential permit is required for TransCanada's May 2012 application for the northern segment of the Keystone XL pipeline, and treats the State Department's 2011 environmental impact statement as satisfying all environmental review law.

Bars the EPA from finalizing Tier 3 vehicle and fuel standards, new petroleum refinery emission rules, and any revision of the ozone air-quality standard until at least 180 days after a new Transportation Fuels Regulatory Committee reports on the cumulative effects of those rules on fuel prices.

Requires the Interior Department to offer at least 25% of newly nominated federal acreage for oil and gas lease sale each year, shields those sales from administrative review, and makes them eligible for environmental categorical exclusions without an extraordinary-circumstances check.
Deems a federal drilling permit approved if Interior has not decided within 60 days, sets a $6,500 processing fee per application, and charges a $5,000 fee for each administrative appeal.

Requires at least one oil and gas lease sale annually in the most prospective parts of the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and fast-track approvals for roads, pipelines, and two new bridges there.

Prohibits the Interior Secretary, through December 31, 2013, from issuing mining regulations that would reduce coal-mine employment, the amount of coal available for mining, or government revenues from coal mining.

Requires offshore wind test-tower permits to be decided within 30 days and exempts those projects from full environmental impact statements; directs 50% of wind and solar right-of-way fees to be retained for processing renewable-energy permits.
Establishes a critical-minerals program including federal resource assessments, permitting coordination, and university grants for workforce training.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed: people living near refineries and in smog-prone areas would wait longer for updated air-quality limits; citizens and conservation groups would face narrower, costlier, shorter avenues to challenge federal land decisions; and the public would get less scrutiny of how federal land and minerals are leased.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near refineries and on smog-prone areas

drawbacks.text: The bill would have delayed finalization of the ozone standard, Tier 3 vehicle and fuel standards, and refinery emission rules for at least six months after a committee report, postponing limits on smog and refinery pollution.

Lease sales of newly nominated federal acreage would be exempt from review and eligible for categorical exclusions without an extraordinary-circumstances check, shortening the environmental review normally required before federal land is leased for drilling.
Drilling permit applications would be automatically approved if Interior misses a 60-day deadline, and administrative appeals would be automatically granted if not reviewed within 60 days.
The bill would require the EPA to weigh feasibility and cost when revising the ozone standard, changing a standard that the Clean Air Act has traditionally set on health grounds.

Litigation over federal energy projects would face a presumption that agency findings are correct, a ban on recovering attorneys' fees, and preliminary injunctions capped at 60 days, making legal challenges harder and more expensive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters billed the bill as a jobs and energy-security package, and faster permitting and pipeline approval could have modestly increased domestic energy activity. But the direct benefits flow mostly to energy producers, while the main costs fall on the public in the form of delayed air-pollution limits, reduced environmental review of public land, and steeper hurdles for citizens to challenge federal energy decisions. The EPA rules it delays were themselves the subject of extensive public comment processes, so the added committee study would have run largely in parallel with analysis the agency already performs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, so it died in committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. John Hoeven introduced the Domestic Energy and Jobs Act on July 26, 2012, with 30 Republican cosponsors including the Republican leader Mitch McConnell.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote was held before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the EPA kept its authority to finalize smog, vehicle-fuel, and refinery standards on its own schedule, and federal land leasing kept full environmental review. Communities that would have borne delayed pollution limits are better off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Air-quality rules and land review stayed intact

for.name: Sen. John Hoeven
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Energy and Jobs Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 30 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Republican leader Mitch McConnell and Energy Committee Republican Lisa Murkowski.

for.name: American Petroleum Institute and fossil-energy groups
for.what_they_did: Backed the 2012 push for Keystone XL approval and expanded federal leasing during the election-year energy debate.

against.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; it sat in committee from July 2012 until the Congress ended.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Had rejected the Keystone XL permit application in January 2012 and opposed congressional attempts to force its approval, making Senate Democratic leaders unwilling to advance the bill.

against.name: Environmental and public-health groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed Keystone XL approval and the bill's delays to EPA clean-air rules, urging senators not to advance it.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led committee and Senate majority never brought the bill up.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and pipeline companies
industries.note: The bill would have approved the Keystone XL pipeline by statute, required annual federal lease sales with less environmental review, and expedited drilling permits and Alaska petroleum-reserve development. Those gains came at the cost of delayed clean-air standards and shortened public review of federal land decisions.

The bill would have barred the EPA from finalizing refinery emission standards for at least six months after a new committee study, deferring compliance costs. The deferred standards limit pollution from refinery communities.
The bill would have barred, through the end of 2013, any mining regulation that would reduce coal employment, minable coal, or coal revenues, shielding the industry from upcoming Interior rules.

The bill would have required 30-day decisions on offshore wind test-tower permits with no environmental impact statement, and directed half of wind and solar right-of-way fees to fund faster permitting of renewables on federal land.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and conservation users of federal land
industries.note: Mandatory lease sales, categorical exclusions without extraordinary-circumstances checks, and new appeal fees would have reduced public input and raised the cost of challenging drilling on land used for recreation, grazing, and habitat.
